task_title: Communications, Light Signals, and Runway Lighting Systems
area: Area III. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can find and set the right frequency, talk to ATC with standard words, use your transponder, read tower light signals, handle a radio failure or emergency, know when to call the NTSB, and read runway and runway status lights.
why: The radio is your link to ATC and other pilots. When it fails, or when words are misheard, you need light signals, the right transponder code and a calm plan.

prereading.what: CTAF, UNICOM, recommended radio calls (Figure 14-1), Chart Supplement, ATIS.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 14, 14-2 to 14-5

prereading.what: Airport lighting, pilot-controlled lighting, RWSL, radio equipment, lost comm, light gun signals, transponder, radar traffic advisories.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 14, 14-16 to 14-26

prereading.what: Non-towered airport calls, ATIS, radar traffic information, radar assistance to VFR, transponder operation.
prereading.label: AIM 4-1-8 to 4-1-20

prereading.what: Radio technique, initial contact, call signs, phonetic alphabet, numbers, radio failure at a tower.
prereading.label: AIM 4-2-1 to 4-2-14

prereading.what: Approach and runway lighting, PAPI/VASI, Runway Status Lights, pilot control of lighting, beacons, taxiway lights.
prereading.label: AIM 2-1-1 to 2-1-10

prereading.what: Emergency authority, distress and urgency calls, 7700 and 7600, VFR aircraft in difficulty.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-1 to 6-4-2

prereading.label: 14 CFR 49 CFR 830.2 to 830.15

warmup: Your radio goes silent 10 miles from a towered airport. How could the tower still clear you to land?

key_terms.def: Common Traffic Advisory Frequency: the frequency pilots use to self-announce at an airport without an operating tower [[1:336|PHAK 14-2]].
Non-government ground radio station at some public airports; can give wind, runway and other info on request [[33:208|AIM 4-1-9e]].
122.9: used to self-announce at airports with no tower, FSS or UNICOM [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g]].
Recorded, looping broadcast of weather and airport info, given a letter code that changes with each update [[1:339|PHAK 14-5]].
ATC's word for setting a code or function on your transponder [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]].
Transponder altitude reporting; sends your altitude in 100-foot steps [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20c]].
I have received your message, understand it, and will comply [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]].
I have received all of your last transmission. Not a yes or no [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]].
Distress / urgency signals, said (preferably) three times at the start of the call [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1c]].
Runway Status Lights: automatic red in-pavement lights (RELs and THLs) that show a runway is unsafe. They are never a clearance [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].
Airport lights you turn on by clicking the mike 7, 5 or 3 times within 5 seconds on a set frequency [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

chunks.title: Find and set the right frequency

body.p: Look up every frequency before you fly. Three main sources: the sectional chart, the Chart Supplement (most complete airport info) and ATIS [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]].

On the sectional, towered airports and their data are blue; others are magenta. The airport block shows the tower (CT) frequency, ATIS, a C symbol after the CTAF, and the UNICOM [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]. A star means the tower is part-time [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].

head: Airport type
Frequency to use
rows: ATIS, then Ground, then Tower. Ground is usually 121.6 to 121.9 MHz [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14c]].

body.p: The CTAF is also listed in the Chart Supplement and on instrument approach charts, or you can ask any FSS [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9b3]]. If no UNICOM info is available, get wind and weather from a nearby ATIS or AWOS [[33:208|AIM 4-1-9f]].

callout.text: Set frequencies early, before you get busy near the airport. Listen to ATIS or AWOS first, then monitor tower or CTAF to picture the traffic [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Radios are VHF: 118.0 to 136.975 MHz and line of sight. Higher altitude means longer range [[1:356|PHAK 14-22]].

check.q: An airport has no tower, no FSS and no UNICOM. Which frequency do you use?

body.p: The most important thing is understanding. Keep it brief, but use whatever words you need to get the message across. Jargon, chatter and "CB" slang have no place [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

bullets: Listen before you transmit. After changing frequency, pause and listen [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2a]].
Think before you key the mike. Know what you will say [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2b]].
Mike close to your lips; normal tone; slight pause after pressing the button [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2c]].
Wait a few seconds before calling again [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2d]].

body.p: Initial call format: (1) who you're calling, (2) your full call sign, (3) your position if on the ground, (4) your request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a]]. Add "information Charlie" if you have the ATIS [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]].

callout.text: Example: "Columbia Ground, Cessna Three One Six Zero Foxtrot, south ramp, I-F-R Memphis." [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a]]. As a student, add "student pilot" on initial contact so ATC can give you extra help [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4c]].

body.p: Call signs: say the type or maker, then the registration, and drop the "N" (e.g., "Bonanza Six Five Five Golf") [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3]]. Never shorten your call sign on initial contact; ATC may shorten it first after contact is made [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a]].

head: Say it like this
Example
rows: 4,500 = "four thousand five hundred"; 12,500 = "one two thousand five hundred" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8, 4-2-9]]

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Received all of your last transmission. Don't use it to answer yes/no [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Received, understand, will comply [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Yes / No [[34:302|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:385|AIM P/C Glossary]]
I can't comply with that instruction or clearance [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Repeat your last transmission [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]]

check.q: Tower asks, "Do you have the field in sight?" Is "Roger" a good answer?
check.a: No. Roger only means you received the message; it should not answer a yes/no question. Say "Affirmative" or "Negative" [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]].

chunks.title: Talk it step by step: a flight with radio calls

body.p: Towered airport, departure and return:

head: Step
What to say or do
rows: Say your position on the airport [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a1]]. Stay on Ground through taxi and run-up, then go to Tower [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14a]].
Always read back the runway assignment, any clearance to enter a runway, and any hold short or line up and wait [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]].
Wait for "cleared for takeoff." You need a clearance to taxi onto a runway, take off or land [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a4]].
Acknowledge first, then switch [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d]]. Leaving radar service? Tell ATC before changing frequency [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]].
Listen to ATIS, then call before entering Class D: two-way radio contact is required first [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)]]. Say "information (letter)" [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13d]].
Stay on Tower until told to contact Ground [[33:258|AIM 4-3-14c]].

body.p: Non-towered airport: monitor and talk on the CTAF from 10 miles out to landing, and from start-up until 10 miles away when departing [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9c1]].

bullets: Inbound: 10 miles out, then entering downwind, base and final, and leaving the runway [[33:207|AIM TBL 4-1-1]].
Outbound: before taxiing and before taxiing onto the runway [[33:207|AIM TBL 4-1-1]].
Say the airport name at the start and end of each call, and use the runway number, not "active runway" [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g8]].
Example: "Strawn traffic, Apache Two Two Five Zulu, (position), (altitude), entering downwind runway one seven, full stop, Strawn" [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g8]].

callout.text: At an airport with an operating tower in Class E or G airspace, contact must be made before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]].

check.q: Ground says, "Cessna 345, taxi to Runway 27 via Alpha, hold short Runway 33." What must your readback include?
check.a: The runway assignment (27) and the hold short of Runway 33, with your call sign [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

body.p: Your transponder answers radar with a four-digit code (4,096 possible) [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20b]]. With Mode C on, it also sends altitude [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20c]].

head: Code
Use
rows: VFR, unless ATC gives you another code [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]]

bullets: On the ground: altitude-reporting mode on any movement area; STBY or OFF at parking [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]].
In controlled airspace: on, with altitude reporting [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a4]].
Press IDENT only when ATC asks [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20d]].
Changing codes: don't pass through 7500, 7600 or 7700. 2700 to 7200? Go 2200 first, then 7200 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].
Give your exact altitude to the nearest 100 ft on initial contact [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20c3]].

callout.text: Mode C and ADS-B Out are required in Class A, B and C; above Class B or C up to 10,000 ft MSL; Class E at and above 10,000 ft MSL (excluding at and below 2,500 ft AGL); and within 30 miles of a Class B primary airport below 10,000 ft MSL (the "Mode C veil") [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f]].

body.p: Radar assistance: all terminal radar facilities give VFR pilots safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectors (workload permitting) and sequencing where set up [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18a]]. Traffic calls give clock position, distance in miles, direction of travel, and type and altitude if known [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15c]].

Clock positions are based on your track, not your heading, so look where you are crabbing [[1:360|PHAK 14-26]] [[33:216|AIM 4-1-15d]]. Vectors are advice: they never let you break a rule, and flying safely is still your job. Tell ATC the weather ahead so you aren't vectored into clouds [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17b-c]]. Advisories don't relieve you of see and avoid [[33:214|AIM 4-1-15]].

check.q: You finish VFR flight following and leave the frequency. What do you do with the transponder?
check.a: Tell ATC before changing frequency, then squawk 1200 [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]].

body.p: If radio contact can't be made, the tower aims a narrow red, white or green light beam at you [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13a]]. The meanings are set by regulation [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

head: Signal
On the ground
In flight
rows: Return for landing (steady green will follow)
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Taxi clear of runway in use
Return to starting point on airport

bullets: Acknowledge in flight: rock your wings by day; blink landing or nav lights at night [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
Acknowledge on the ground by day: move ailerons or rudder; at night blink landing or nav lights [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].
At night on the ground, to get the tower's attention: turn on the landing light and taxi clear of the active runway where the tower can see it [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13c]].
Limits: you may not be looking when they flash you, and lights can only approve or deny what you seem to be doing [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13b]].

callout.text: Green = go. Red = no. Flashing red = get off the runway, or don't land at all. White = go home (to the ramp). Red and green together = careful!

check.q: You are on final with no radio. The tower shows a steady red light. What do you do?
check.a: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

body.p: First, check the simple things. Many "failures" are equipment or set-up issues:

bullets: Volume down, wrong frequency, or a stuck mike blocking the frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2e]].
Out of range: VHF is line of sight; climb for better range [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2f]].
Audio panel set to the wrong radio or speaker. Switching the transmitter selector between COM1 and COM2 changes both transmit and receive [[23:53|IFH 2-2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
Electrical trouble: an ammeter on the minus side means more current is used than replaced; full-scale minus means the alternator has failed [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

After an alternator failure the battery may last only about 30 to 40 minutes (a rough number, not to be relied on). Turn off unneeded equipment and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].
Recheck your radios or try the other transmitter [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3a3]]. If you still can't reach anyone, call "ANY RADIO" and ask for a call back on a frequency you can use [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3b3]].

body.p: Squawk 7600 for a loss of two-way radio [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

head: Problem (arriving at a tower)
What to do
rows: Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the traffic flow. Tell the tower your type, position, altitude, that you'll land, and ask for light signals. At 3 to 5 miles, report position, join the pattern and watch for lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]].
Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern, monitor tower, watch for lights. Rock wings (day) or blink lights (night) to acknowledge [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]].
Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern, keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]].

callout.text: VFR radio failure in Class D: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land (a steady green) [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]].

bullets: Radio dead before leaving the ramp? Get it fixed. If you can't, phone the tower and ask to depart without two-way radio [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]].
Busy airports don't accept no-radio arrivals [[1:357|PHAK 14-23]]. Landing at a quieter non-towered airport may be wiser; watch extra carefully there [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]].

check.q: Your receiver works but your transmitter doesn't. How do you acknowledge the tower in daylight while flying?

chunks.title: Declaring an emergency, and reporting afterward

body.p: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about position, fuel, weather, or anything else that could hurt flight safety. Ask for help then, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]]. Delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2b]].

head: Distress
Urgency
rows: Grave, imminent danger; need immediate help [[34:377|AIM P/C Glossary]]

bullets: Climb if you can, for better radio and radar coverage.
Talking to ATC already? Keep your code. If not, squawk 7700 with Mode C.
Call on the frequency in use, or 121.5 if needed [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1h]].
Say: MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, station, call sign and type, problem, weather, intentions, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board.

callout.text: VFR pilot in difficulty near clouds: choose a route that keeps you in VFR. If you can't stay VFR, tell ATC you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]].

In an emergency you may deviate from any Part 91 rule as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. If you deviate from an ATC clearance, tell ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]. If ATC asks: a written report to the FAA for a rule deviation [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]], or a detailed report within 48 hours to the ATC facility manager if you were given priority [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]].

body.p: NTSB reporting. An accident is death, serious injury, or substantial damage between boarding for flight and everyone getting off [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Substantial damage does not include engine-only damage, bent fairings or cowlings, dented skin, small punctures, or damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].
Notify the NTSB immediately for an accident, an overdue aircraft believed to be in an accident [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5(b)]], or serious incidents such as [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)]]:

bullets: Flight control system malfunction or failure
A required crewmember can't do their duties due to injury or illness
In-flight fire
Aircraft collision in flight
Damage to other property estimated over $25,000
Serious injury includes hospital stay over 48 hours (starting within 7 days), most bone fractures, second- or third-degree burns, or burns over 5 percent of the body [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]].
Don't move wreckage except to help people, protect it, or protect the public [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].
File NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days of an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing. For an incident, only if asked [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

check.q: On a cross-country you're unsure of your position and fuel is getting tight. Is it too early to call for help?
check.a: No. Doubt about position or fuel already puts you in at least an urgency condition; ask for help now [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]].

head: Light
What it looks like
rows: White and green: land airport. White and yellow: water airport. Green, yellow and white: heliport. Military: two quick white flashes between greens [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9]]
White. On instrument runways, yellow on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
Red toward the runway; green outward to landing aircraft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4c]]
Pair of synchronized flashing lights at the threshold [[33:126|AIM 2-1-3]]
White until the last 3,000 ft, then alternating red/white for the next 2,000 ft, and all red in the last 1,000 ft [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]]

body.p: PAPI: a row of 2 or 4 lights, normally on the left side. Two white and two red means on glide path (3 degrees); more white is high, more red is low. Visible about 5 miles by day and up to 20 at night; safe obstacle clearance within 10 degrees of centerline out to 3.4 NM [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]]. Don't start down until lined up with the runway [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].
Pilot-controlled lighting: at selected airports, key the mike on the published frequency [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]:

bullets: Always key 7 times first, then adjust down. Lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8b-c]].
The frequency (often the CTAF) is in the Chart Supplement and on approach charts, not on sectionals [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8d]].
On the sectional, "*L" means lighting limits (e.g., pilot-controlled); check the Chart Supplement [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].

callout.text: A beacon on in daytime in a surface area often means weather below 1,000 ft ceiling or 3 miles visibility, but there's no requirement. Don't rely on it; check the weather [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9d]].

check.q: On final you see three red and one white on the PAPI. What does it mean?
check.a: Slightly low (about 2.8 degrees). Fly up to two white, two red [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]].

body.p: RWSL is fully automatic. It uses surveillance data to turn on red in-pavement lights when it is unsafe to enter, cross, take off from or land on a runway. It never gives a clearance; you still need one from ATC [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6a]].

head: Lights
Where
Red means
rows: On the taxiway centerline from the hold line to the runway [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]]
High-speed traffic on the runway, or an aircraft on final within the activation area (about 1 mile out, adjustable) [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b]]
Two rows along the runway centerline, 1,500 ft long, starting 375 ft from the departure threshold [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]]
Unsafe to take off: the runway is occupied or about to be [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c]]

bullets: See red RELs: stop at the hold line or stay stopped, and call ATC if your clearance conflicts [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b4]].
See red THLs: stop if safe, or stay stopped, and call ATC [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c3]].
Never cross illuminated red lights [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d3]].
Lights going out is NOT a clearance [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d4]].
Keep the transponder/ADS-B on from leaving parking until shutdown so the system can see you [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d1]].

check.q: You're cleared to cross Runway 9, but the RELs in front of you turn red. What now?
check.a: Stop at the hold line and tell ATC the lights conflict with your clearance; never cross illuminated red lights [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6b4]] [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Hearing what you expect (expectation bias), e.g., a runway change you read but still pictured the old way [[30:45|RMH 6-2]]
Read back runways and hold shorts every time; if unsure, ask [[33:261|AIM 4-3-18a9]]
Taking a clearance meant for a similar call sign
Use your full call sign in readbacks; say "verify clearance for (your call sign)" if in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]]
"Have numbers" said to mean you have the ATIS
"Have numbers" means wind, runway and altimeter only; it does not mean you have ATIS [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]]
Not a recognized phrase; don't use it [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g1]]
Controller can't tell if you have radio failure; acknowledge first [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3d1]]
Request clarification right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]; say "unable" if you can't comply [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]

body.p: Non-standard words cause misunderstandings. Good phraseology is the mark of a professional; study the Pilot/Controller Glossary [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1c]]. Read back altitudes, vectors and runway assignments so the numbers get double-checked [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]].

callout.text: ATC will not use the word "cleared" in taxi instructions. A taxi route to a runway does NOT let you enter or cross it [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]].

check.q: You hear a clearance and aren't sure it was for you; another plane has a similar call sign. What do you say?
check.a: "Verify clearance for" your full call sign [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a2]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: find the frequency you need

body.p: Look up frequencies before you fly, not while you are busy in the cockpit. Airports with control towers are marked CT with the primary tower frequency. A table on the chart border gives more: the tower hours in local time, then tower, ground control and ATIS frequencies [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]] [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

Read across one row at a time. Some frequencies depend on the runway in use or on approach direction. The letters ASR or PAR mean a radar instrument approach is published. A second table lists approach control frequencies for Class B, Class C and TRSA, sometimes split by sector [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

Next to the airport symbol you get a data block. CT is the tower frequency. ATIS is the recorded airport information. A number in italics, such as 122.95, is the UNICOM or advisory station. The long number before it, like 72, is the longest runway in hundreds of feet, and the usable length may be less [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

A circled C after the tower frequency means the airport follows the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency. RP means right traffic on the listed runways. A star means a part-time operation, so check the tower table for hours [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

f8.alt: Two sample airport data blocks, one magenta and one blue, with callouts for the rotating beacon and UNICOM, above a two-column list of items: FSS on field, NO SVFR, FAR 93 box, identifiers, CT 118.3, a star for part-time operation, a circled C for CTAF, ATIS 123.8, AFIS 135.2, ASOS or AWOS 135.42, elevation 285, lighting L, longest runway 72, UNICOM 122.95, RP 23,34, VFR Advsy 125.0, weather camera and airport of entry.

scenario.title: Fading radio on the way home
scenario.setup: You're a student pilot on a solo cross-country, 20 miles from your home airport in Class D airspace. The weather is good VFR. The ammeter needle sits on the minus side, the low-voltage light comes on, and Approach's voice is getting faint. Then the radio goes quiet.

questions.q: What does the ammeter tell you, and how long can you count on the battery?
questions.a: Minus means more current is drawn than replaced; full-scale minus means the alternator has failed [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. The battery might last about 30 to 40 minutes, but that is only a rough guess. Shed load and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

questions.q: Is this an emergency? Should you say so?
questions.a: Whether radio failure is an emergency is your call [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1b]]. Doubt about your situation already means at least urgency; ask for help early, while the radio still works [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]]. A short "PAN-PAN" call with your problem and intentions is fine [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

questions.q: The radio is now dead. What code do you squawk?
How do you get into your Class D airport?
questions.a: Stay outside or above the surface area until you know the traffic flow, join the pattern, and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a3]]. You may land in basic VFR with visual contact and a clearance to land, a steady green [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]]. A quieter non-towered airport may be a better choice [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]].

questions.q: On downwind you get a flashing green, then on final a steady red. What do they mean?
questions.a: Flashing green: return for landing; steady red: give way to other aircraft and continue circling [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

questions.q: Earlier, before the failure, you told Approach "we're good, gonna head home." What was wrong with that?
questions.a: It is slang, not standard phraseology, and leaves ATC guessing. Use standard words and say exactly what you need [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1b-c]], e.g., your problem, intentions and request [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a3]].

skills.do: Find the right frequencies for each phase (ATIS, Ground, Tower or CTAF, Approach) on the chart and Chart Supplement, set them in the radio and select the right COM on the audio panel.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write a frequency list for both airports. In the plane, say each frequency out loud as you set it.

skills.do: Make calls in standard AIM/P-C Glossary format: who you're calling, who you are, where you are, what you want.
skills.practice: Chair-fly a full flight's radio calls at home. Listen to a live tower feed and repeat calls in your head.

skills.do: Acknowledge every call with your call sign, read back runways, hold shorts and altitudes, and comply (or say "unable").
skills.practice: Have your CFI play ATC on the ground, including hold-short instructions and frequency changes, until readbacks are automatic.

quiz.q: You are on the ground with no radio. The tower shows you a flashing green light. What does it mean?
options: Cleared for takeoff
Cleared to taxi
Return to starting point
Taxi clear of the runway in use
quiz.why: Flashing green to an aircraft on the surface means cleared to taxi [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

quiz.q: In flight, the tower shows a flashing red light. What does it mean?
options: Give way and continue circling
Airport unsafe, do not land
Return for landing
Exercise extreme caution
quiz.why: Flashing red in flight means airport unsafe, do not land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

quiz.q: Which transponder code shows a loss of two-way radio?
quiz.why: Squawk 7600 for loss of two-way radio [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

quiz.q: At a pilot-controlled lighting airport, what should you do first?
options: Key the mike 3 times in 5 seconds
Key the mike 5 times in 5 seconds
Call UNICOM to turn on the lights
Key the mike 7 times in 5 seconds
quiz.why: Always key 7 times first for full brightness, then adjust down. Lights stay on 15 minutes [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8b-c]].

quiz.q: You are lined up on the runway with a takeoff clearance and the Takeoff Hold Lights turn red. What do you do?
options: Take off; you have a clearance
Stay stopped and contact ATC
Wait until the lights go out, then go without calling
Flash your landing light
quiz.why: Red THLs mean unsafe to take off. Stay stopped and contact ATC if the lights conflict with your clearance [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6c3]]. Lights going out is not a clearance [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d4]].

quiz.q: Which event requires immediate NTSB notification?
options: A flat tire on landing
A bent wingtip from a hangar door
An in-flight fire
Engine damage limited to one engine
quiz.why: In-flight fire is a listed serious incident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)(4)]]. Tire, wingtip and engine-only damage are not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]].

quiz.q: A 4-light PAPI shows two white and two red. You are:
options: On the glide path
Slightly above
Well above the glide path
Slightly below
quiz.why: Two white, two red = on glide path (3 degrees) [[33:124|AIM FIG 2-1-5]].

quiz.q: You become unsure of your position and fuel. According to the AIM, you are in:
options: A normal condition until the engine quits
A distress condition only if ATC agrees
At least an urgency condition
No emergency unless you are IFR
quiz.why: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about position or fuel; ask for help then [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]].

quiz.q: On the tower table, what is the ATIS frequency for Cox Dayton Intl?
quiz.why: In the Cox Dayton Intl row the ATIS column shows 125.8. 119.9 is the tower frequency and 121.9 is ground [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: The tower table marks Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky Intl's tower frequencies as "Runway dependent." What does that mean for you?
options: You must call ground control before every call
The tower talks only to IFR traffic in the area
The tower works only on some days of the week
The frequency you call depends on the runway in use
quiz.why: The note beside the Cincinnati tower frequencies says runway dependent, so you choose the frequency for the runway in use [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: The tower table lists hours of operation for each airport. In what time are they given?
options: UTC
The time of the last ATIS
Eastern time at every airport
Local time
quiz.why: The chart notes say that operational hours are local time [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: On the airport data legend, which frequency does the figure label UNICOM?
quiz.why: The arrow labeled UNICOM points to the italic number 122.95. 123.8 is ATIS, 118.3 is the tower and 125.0 is VFR advisory [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

quiz.q: The legend shows a small circled C after CT - 118.3. What does it mean?
options: It marks the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency
A weather camera is mounted on the airport
The tower is closed during the night hours
The airport is also an airport of entry
quiz.why: The circled C follows the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

quiz.q: A tower controller tells you to enter a right base. You would like a straight-in instead. Under 14 CFR 91.123(b), what is the rule?
options: Except in an emergency, you may not go against an ATC instruction
You may ignore it once you have the airport in sight and in range
You may ignore it if you are flying VFR in good weather conditions
You may ignore it if following it adds extra time and fuel burn
quiz.why: [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]] says that except in an emergency, no person may operate an aircraft contrary to an ATC instruction in an area where ATC is exercised. Ask for what you want and follow the answer.

takeaways: Get frequencies from the chart, Chart Supplement and ATIS before you fly; CTAF from 10 miles out.
Standard calls: who you call, who you are, where you are, what you want. Read back runways and hold shorts.
Squawk 1200 VFR, 7600 lost radio, 7700 emergency, never 7777.
Light guns: green go, red no, flashing red don't land or get off the runway, flashing white back to the ramp.
Ask for help early; doubt means urgency. Notify the NTSB at once for accidents and listed serious incidents.
Red RWSL lights mean stop, even with a clearance; lights going out is not a clearance.
cfi_notes: Examiners often show a light gun card and ask for the meaning on the ground vs. in flight. Drill the two columns separately; students mix up flashing green (taxi / return for landing) and flashing red (clear the runway / don't land).
Have the student build a frequency list from the Chart Supplement for an unfamiliar towered and non-towered airport, including the PCL frequency, which is not on the sectional (AIM 2-1-8d).
Practice lost-comm by turning the volume down in flight (safely) and having the student run the full sequence: troubleshoot, squawk 7600, plan entry, recite light signals.
Common student mistakes: saying "Roger" to yes/no questions, using "have numbers" to mean ATIS, saying "traffic in the area please advise", and not reading back hold short instructions.

Source differences (lesson follows the AIM/regs): PHAK Figure 14-44 says pilot A sees traffic at 1 o'clock; AIM FIG 4-1-1 (AIM 4-1-15d) says 2 o'clock for the same picture, so the figure caption gives the AIM answer. The point is the same: calls are based on track. PHAK 14-18 calls the caution-zone runway edge lights amber; AIM 2-1-4 and AFH 11-7 say yellow. 14 CFR 91.125 says "cleared to taxi"; AIM TBL 4-3-1 says "cleared for taxi".

The ACS lists only K9 (Runway Status Lighting Systems) for lighting, but the Task title covers runway lighting systems, so the lighting chunk covers edge, end, centerline, PAPI, beacon and PCL basics too. This Task has no R3 element.
gaps: K6 equipment issues: sources cover volume, frequency, stuck mike, range, audio panel/COM selection and alternator failure, but not hands-on troubleshooting like checking headset plugs or a failed push-to-talk switch. Aircraft-specific steps (electrical failure checklist, battery time, audio panel use) come from the POH.
Fly it step by step: the AFH has no radio-call procedure, so the step-by-step chunk is built from the AIM (4-1-9, 4-1-13, 4-3-14, 4-3-18).
RWSL deployment: PHAK 14-19 gives 2016 status only (14 airports); current RWSL airport list is not in these sources.
No specific ACS tolerances in this Task's Skills elements; the examiner judges standard phraseology and compliance.

activities.title: Leaving a towered airport: calls in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Listen to ATIS and note the letter code
Call Ground with your position on the airport and the ATIS letter
Read back the runway and any hold short instruction
Taxi and do the run-up while staying on Ground
Switch to Tower and say you are ready for takeoff
Taxi onto the runway only after Tower clears you

activities.title: Which squawk?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap the code you should squawk.

items.t: VFR cross-country, not talking to ATC
You just told ATC you are leaving flight following
Your radio quits, but the transponder still works
You can't transmit or receive on either radio
Engine fire, and you can't reach any ATC facility yet
Lost and low on fuel, not in contact with anyone
On flight following, Approach assigned you code 5231
Flying through Class C on the code Approach gave you

activities.title: Read the light gun
activities.intro: Tap a light signal, then what it means.

pairs.r: Return for landing; a steady green will follow
Give way to other aircraft and keep circling
Taxi clear of the runway in use
Return to your starting point on the airport

activities.title: True or false: emergencies and lights

cards.s: A PAN-PAN call has priority over a MAYDAY call.
cards.why: No. Urgency (PAN-PAN) calls come before everything except distress. A MAYDAY call always goes first [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1d]].

cards.s: Saying MAYDAY tells everyone else on the frequency to stay quiet.
cards.why: Yes. Distress calls have absolute priority, and MAYDAY commands radio silence on the frequency in use [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1d]].

cards.s: A flight control system failure must be reported to the NTSB right away, even if nothing was damaged.
cards.why: Yes. It is a listed serious incident that needs immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)(1)]].

cards.s: If the airport beacon is on in daytime, the weather must be below VFR minimums.
cards.why: No. It often means that, but there is no rule requiring it. Don't rely on the beacon; check the weather [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9d]].

cards.s: On a runway with centerline lights, all the centerline lights are red in the last 1,000 feet.
cards.why: Yes. They are white, then alternate red and white for 2,000 feet, then all red for the last 1,000 feet [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]].

cards.s: When red Runway Entrance Lights turn off, you may cross the runway without a clearance.
cards.why: No. Lights going out is not a clearance. RWSL only confirms a clearance from ATC; it never replaces one [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d4]].

activities.title: Read the airport data legend
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

final_quiz.q: Look at the sample airport data. The tower is part-time and closed tonight, and the airport has no FSS open. Which frequency do you use to self-announce?
options: 122.95, the UNICOM
123.8, the ATIS
122.9, MULTICOM
118.3, the tower frequency
final_quiz.why: The star means the tower is part-time, and the circled C after 118.3 marks it as the CTAF [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]. When the tower is closed, self-announce on the CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g2]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a Piper Cherokee, registration N7284R. How do you say your call sign on first contact with the tower?
options: Cherokee November Seven Two Eight Four Romeo
Eight Four Romeo
Cherokee Seventy-Two Eighty-Four Romeo
Cherokee Seven Two Eight Four Romeo
final_quiz.why: Say the type or maker, then the registration digit by digit, and drop the N [[33:230|AIM 4-2-4a3]]. Never shorten your call sign on first contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1]].

final_quiz.q: You are VFR on flight following. Approach tells you to climb to 5,500 feet, but a cloud layer at 5,000 feet is in the way. What do you say?
options: "Unable" and tell them about the clouds
"Roger" and hold altitude without mentioning the clouds
"Affirmative" and climb into the clouds as directed
"Wilco" and climb while trying to stay out of clouds
final_quiz.why: "Unable" means you can't comply with an instruction [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]. ATC help never lets you break a rule, and you should keep ATC told about the weather ahead [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17b-c]]. "Wilco" would promise to comply [[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]].

final_quiz.q: Ground says, "Cessna Five Two Kilo, Runway 24, taxi via Alpha." You reach the end of Alpha at Runway 24. What now?
options: Taxi onto Runway 24; the taxi instruction covers it since it names the runway
Say "taking the active" and line up when you see the runway is clear
Line up on Runway 24 if no one is on final and you have looked both ways
Stop short and get a clearance from Tower before entering the runway
final_quiz.why: A taxi route to your departure runway does not let you enter or cross it [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a6]]. You need a clearance to taxi onto a runway or take off while the tower is open [[33:260|AIM 4-3-18a4]].

final_quiz.q: You are squawking 4632. ATC tells you to squawk 7213. What is the best way to change the code?
options: Change the first digit to 7 first, then the rest
Pass through 7700 quickly, then set 7213
Set 4213 first, then change the first digit to 7
Pass through 7600 quickly, then set 7213
final_quiz.why: Avoid landing on 7500 or any 7600 or 7700 code, even for a moment. Changing the 4 first would give 7632, a 7600-series code that sets off an alarm. Change the other digits first, then the 7 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20e1]].

final_quiz.q: You plan to fly VFR at 3,500 feet MSL, 25 miles from the primary airport of a Class B area, staying outside the Class B. What equipment do you need?
options: An operating Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out
Nothing extra, since you stay outside the Class B airspace
Only a working two-way radio and a current sectional chart
A Class B clearance from ATC before you fly near the area
final_quiz.why: Within 30 miles of a Class B primary airport, below 10,000 feet MSL (the "Mode C veil"), you need Mode C and ADS-B Out [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f2]].

final_quiz.q: It is night. You are taxiing with a dead radio and the tower shines a flashing white light at you. What does it mean, and how do you answer?
options: Cleared to taxi; blink your landing or nav lights, since it is night
Return to your starting point; blink your landing or nav lights
Return to your starting point; move the ailerons to acknowledge
Exercise extreme caution; rock your wings to show that you understand
final_quiz.why: Flashing white on the ground means return to starting point on the airport [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. At night you acknowledge by blinking the landing or navigation lights; moving the ailerons is for daytime [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

final_quiz.q: At the ramp of a towered airport, you find your only radio is dead. What should you do?
options: Take off and squawk 7600 right away, since a dead radio is a comm failure
Get it fixed; if you can't, phone the tower and ask to depart without a radio
Taxi to the runway and wait for a steady green light before you depart
Depart and call the tower on 121.5 once you are airborne and clear
final_quiz.why: Make every effort to get the radio fixed. If you can't, call the tower by phone and ask for approval to depart without two-way radio [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13b]].

final_quiz.q: You are VFR on flight following and not instrument rated. Clouds close in ahead and around you, and you can't find any way to stay in VFR conditions. What should you do?
options: Squawk 7600 and turn toward home, staying low to keep the ground in sight
Ask for vectors through the clouds without mentioning your rating
Tell ATC you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition
Wait until you are in the clouds before saying anything to ATC
final_quiz.why: If you can't continue in VFR conditions, tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b2]]. Asking early is the key [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2a]].

final_quiz.q: While taxiing for takeoff with a passenger, your wingtip hits a parked fuel truck. No one is hurt. Your airplane has only a bent wingtip, but the truck repair is estimated at $40,000. What do you do?
options: Nothing; a bent wingtip is not substantial damage
Tell the airport manager only
File an NTSB report within 10 days, with no call needed
Notify the NTSB immediately
final_quiz.why: Damage to property other than the aircraft, estimated at more than $25,000 to repair, is a listed serious incident that needs immediate NTSB notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)(6)]]. A bent wingtip is not substantial damage, so this is not an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], but the truck damage alone makes the call required.

final_quiz.q: You are landing at night on a long instrument runway. Near the far end, the runway edge lights change from white to yellow. What does that tell you?
options: You are in the last 2,000 feet, or the last half if that is less
The runway is closed ahead
You are near a taxiway exit
You are past the touchdown zone and must go around
final_quiz.why: On instrument runways, yellow edge lights replace white on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less. They form a caution zone for landings [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4b]].

final_quiz.q: You fly into an airport that has Runway Status Lights. When should your transponder and ADS-B Out be on?
options: Only once you are airborne and have been cleared for takeoff by the tower
Only while you are on a runway or crossing a hold-short line
From leaving parking until you shut down at parking
Only when ATC asks for it on the frequency before you taxi
final_quiz.why: At RWSL airports, keep the transponder and ADS-B on from the moment you leave the parking area until you shut down there, so the system can see you [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d1]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot calls the tower and says, "have numbers." What does that tell the controller?
options: The pilot has the field in sight and can follow traffic
The pilot has the current ATIS and needs no other information
The pilot has wind, runway and altimeter only
The pilot knows the traffic pattern altitude and entry point
final_quiz.why: "Have numbers" means only wind, runway and altimeter. It does not mean you have the ATIS; say "information (letter)" for that [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]].

final_quiz.q: On the airport data legend, what does RP 23,34 mean?
options: Radar approach on runways 23 and 34
Right traffic patterns on runways 23 and 34
Restricted parking on runways 23 and 34
Runways 23 and 34 are rough
final_quiz.why: RP means runways with right traffic patterns. An asterisk before it means see the Chart Supplement [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

final_quiz.q: In the sample block 285 L 72 122.95, what does 72 tell you?
options: The tower closes at 7:20 local time each night of the week
The airport elevation is only 72 ft above sea level here
The magnetic heading of the main runway is 072 degrees
The longest runway is about 7,200 ft; usable length may be less
final_quiz.why: The number is the length of the longest runway in hundreds of feet. Usable length may be less [[2:24|Chart Users' Guide p 24]].

final_quiz.q: You deviated from an ATC clearance during an emergency. What does 14 CFR 91.123(c) require next?
options: Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible
Call ATC only if the FAA asks you to
File a report within 90 days
Nothing, because an emergency removes all duties
final_quiz.why: A pilot in command who deviates from an ATC clearance or instruction in an emergency must notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]].
